New Mexico Income Support Division seeks 10.6% budget bump to offset feds’ SNAP cuts By Margaret O'Hara, Searchlight New Mexico November 17, 2026

New Mexico Income Support Division seeks 10.6% budget bump to offset feds’ SNAP cuts

By Margaret O'Hara, Searchlight New Mexico
November 17, 2026

The Income Support Division of the New Mexico Health Care Authority has requested a budget increase of nearly 11% in the next fiscal year to address the effects of coming federal cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. 

Federal changes to SNAP stem from a sweeping 2025 budget reconciliation law that slashed taxes and discretionary spending through 2034, with cuts to food assistance and Medicaid among its key cost-saving measures. The law is expected to kick 58,000 New Mexicans off SNAP and 88,000 off Medicaid.

For the state Health Care Authority, the law translates to more work and higher costs, Cabinet Secretary Kari Armijo told members of the Legislative Finance Committee on Monday.

“The impacts of H.R. 1 are not just policy impacts or financial impacts. They are workload impacts for our agency,” she said. “We have to equate all of this work into tasks and a frontline workforce that can manage those tasks.”

New Mexico has the highest SNAP participation rate in the country, according to data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. More than one in five of the state’s residents relies on the program to keep food on the table.

The Income Support Division — which administers the food assistance program in New Mexico — is seeking $146.8 million for fiscal year 2028, an increase of about $14 million from the current fiscal year, or 10.6%.

The request includes $5 million in recurring funds to shore up local food banks, which have been working to fill the gap as customers have started to drop off SNAP rolls. However, food banks can’t replace SNAP: For every one meal provided by a food bank, SNAP provides nine, according to estimates from the nationwide food bank network Feeding America.

The proposed budget also would set aside $6.7 million to cover the state’s increased portion of SNAP administrative costs. The state now has to pay half the administrative expenses of running the program, while previously it paid for a quarter of the costs.

In addition, the Health Care Authority asked lawmakers to increase the budget for its financial, administrative and information technology arm, which also will be involved in implementing changes to SNAP.

The SNAP program has seen a year of unprecedented turmoil. The Trump administration initially refused to issue benefits in November 2025, amid a federal government shutdown. The governor and state Legislature stepped up during that period of uncertainty, providing first a $30 million stopgap for 10 days and then authorizing up to $162.5 million to continue the program, if necessary, during a speedy special legislative session.

The program changed again in January, when some 55,000 New Mexicans had to start complying with new work requirements to maintain their SNAP benefits.

State costs for the SNAP program will continue to rise as a result of the federal budget reconciliation law — just not yet.

New Mexico’s payment error rate — a measure that accounts for both over- and underpayment of benefits — was so high that the state will not have to start paying for even more SNAP-related costs until late 2029. If the state fails to significantly reduce its payment error rate, however, New Mexico is set to lose up to $173 million in federal funding annually, according to a Legislative Finance Committee evaluation.
